Franklyn / United States v. Gonzalez — Gonzalez's ammunition conviction rests on a distinct supply-and-recipient connection](HOLDINGS.md#gonzalezs-ammunition-conviction-rests-on-a-distinct-supply-and-recipient-connection); [United States v. Griffin / United States v. Langley — The supply restriction and recipient-possession rule supply the constitutional connection](HOLDINGS.md#the-supply-restriction-and-recipient-possession-rule-supply-the-constitutional-connection-1); [United States v. Griffin / United States v. Langley — The requested direct-effect instruction would add an element](HOLDINGS.md#the-requested-direct-effect-instruction-would-add-an-element-1).

## Standards and Tests selection: Compulsory state executive administration of federal private-party regulation

### Compulsory state executive administration of federal private-party regulation

**Governing question:** Whether Congress may command unwilling state executive officers to perform affirmative duties as administrators of a federal regulatory program directed at private persons.

**Current rule:** Congress may regulate private conduct within its enumerated powers, preempt conflicting state law and use federal institutions to enforce federal obligations. The Commerce and Necessary and Proper Clauses do not authorize it to command unwilling state executive officers to perform affirmative investigative, screening or enforcement duties as administrators of a federal regulatory program directed at private persons, including the records research and implicit required acceptance of the dealer's notice and the purchaser's statement that §922(s)(2)'s mandatory inquiry entails. The defect is compulsory assignment of executive responsibility, not the number of hours required or the absence of federal reimbursement. The rule rests on structural federalism and is categorical: no case-by-case balancing of burdens and benefits applies. Reasonable-effort limits, a designee option, temporary duration, modest effort or retained local discretion do not make the duty voluntary, and the violation does not depend on proof of cost, a state-law prohibition or personal liability; an assumed promise of reimbursement would not cure it.

**Authority by component:**
- Categorical structural rule and its application to the mandatory inquiry: Printz/Mack, Printz v. United States / Mack v. United States — Part I — Congress may not command unwilling state executive officers to administer federal regulation of private persons, Thomas with Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy (five), 1997-06-27. O'Connor does not join Part I's reach to purely ministerial reporting or record-processing requirements.

**Present operation effective:** Printz/Mack, 1997-06-27.

**Exceptions and limits:** The rule does not prohibit direct federal regulation of state activity or generally applicable laws, duties assigned to state courts as courts under the Supremacy Clause, voluntary cooperation or otherwise valid conditional federal spending, and it does not limit Congress's authority to regulate the underlying transactions. Garcia, Baker, Testa and Howlett are preserved, and FERC v. Mississippi remains within its bounded regulatory and adjudicative setting. The rule is not a physical-occupation rule, an individual-rights scrutiny standard or a totality test, and it rests on no Take Care or unity-of-the-executive holding. Duties under constitutional grants specifically involving state governmental action, including federal elections; actual consent to cooperative arrangements; statutory compensation agreements; and the complete rights of nonparty dealers remain unresolved. The decision creates no compensation rule, no individual Second Amendment holding and no new substantive severability rule.

**Open question:** Whether purely ministerial reporting or record-processing requirements imposed on unwilling state executive officers fall within the prohibition has no Court answer: O'Connor reserves it, and Part I's reach to such duties is the opinion of four Justices only (Thomas with Stone-Zsela, Scalia and Kennedy).

**Related current rules:** “Compulsory state regulation or ownership of private obligations” remains intact, and this rule extends its structural prohibition from compulsory legislation and ownership to compulsory executive administration; valid preemption, generally applicable regulation, voluntary cooperation, lawful spending arrangements and the distinct sources of state-court and election duties retain their own boundaries.

**Controlling construction:** Section 922(s)(2) requires reasonable effort within five business days after the dealer notice, including available State, local and designated national records. It commands no arrest, prosecution, prevention of a transfer or adverse dealer notification. Under (6)(B), unless the transaction is determined unlawful, the transmitted purchaser statement, derived-information records and notice-created records must be destroyed within twenty business days after the statement was made; disclosure is confined to a person needing the information to carry out the subsection and use to that purpose. The same unlawful-transaction exception qualifies those information restrictions. Under the separate (6)(C), written reasons are due only after an ineligibility determination and the individual's request, within twenty business days after receipt of that request. With the mandatory checks removed, these conditional provisions compel no participation from officers who decline the program and are not separately declared invalid; their operation after voluntary participation is not decided, and no officer receives a general license to retain, use or disclose information.

**Holdings navigation:** Printz v. United States; Mack v. United States (1997-06-27) — Part I — Congress may not command unwilling state executive officers to administer federal regulation of private persons; Printz v. United States; Mack v. United States (1997-06-27) — Part I — Reach to purely ministerial record-processing (opinion of four Justices).

## Standards and Tests selection: Federal-law transfer restrictions and exclusion of trust interests

### Federal-law transfer restrictions and exclusion of trust interests

**Governing question:** Exclusion of a debtor's beneficial trust interest from the estate under 11 U.S.C. §541(c)(2).

**Current rule:** Applicable nonbankruptcy law includes federal law. A transfer restriction on a debtor's beneficial interest in a trust is preserved when enforceable under that law; an established ERISA-qualified trust with an ERISA-enforceable antialienation restriction is therefore excluded from the estate. Exclusion is distinct from exemption and does not change exemption deadlines or adjudicate statutory avoidance remedies.

**Authority by component:**
- Federal-law construction and qualifying trust exclusion: Patterson v. Shumate, “Holding 1: An enforceable federal pension restriction excludes this beneficial trust interest”, June 15, 1992; Blackmun, joined by White, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas (eight).

**Present operation effective:** Patterson v. Shumate, June 15, 1992.

**Open question:** Other plans, nontrust interests, statutory exceptions, distributed benefits, §522(b)(2)(A) and the payment-versus-corpus scope of §522(d)(10)(E) are not decided.

**Holdings navigation:** Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992) — Estate exclusions for pension trust interests.

## Standards and Tests selection: Independent recovery of collateral-preservation expenses under section 506(c)

### Independent recovery of collateral-preservation expenses under section 506(c)

**Governing question:** Who may independently seek a section 506(c) surcharge.

**Current rule:** Only the trustee, including a debtor in possession exercising the trustee’s statutory powers, may independently recover under section 506(c) reasonable and necessary costs of preserving or disposing of property securing an allowed secured claim, to the extent of benefit to its holder. Administrative-claimant status, asserted collateral benefit and chapter 11 participation do not give another claimant that independent cause of action.

**Authority by component:**

- Hartford Underwriters Insurance Co. v. Union Planters Bank, N.A.; No. 99-409. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, Section 506(c) gives the independent recovery power to the trustee, 2000-05-30; Thomas with all eight other Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 2000-05-30; the component authority identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** Authorized derivative pursuit, assignment, an actual trustee recovery and its allocation, recovery before paying an expense, and separate remedies remain reserved. The rule neither abolishes statutory bankruptcy equity nor determines administrative allowance or actual benefit.


## Selected additional Holdings authority

### Federal tolling of supplemental state-law claims

#### Jinks v. Richland County, 538 U.S. 456

**Docket or dockets:** No. 02-258.
**Decided:** April 22, 2003.

##### Valid federal tolling of qualifying supplemental claims

**Holding:** Section 1367(d) is a necessary and proper means of administering authorized federal adjudication and binds state courts as to qualifying supplemental claims, including these claims against Richland County. It tolls the limitations period for a claim asserted under subsection (a), and any other claim in the same action voluntarily dismissed at the same time as or after dismissal of a subsection (a) claim, while pending and for thirty days after dismissal unless state law provides a longer tolling period.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion of the Court, unanimous.

**Material application:** The claim-linked period allows lawful use of §1367(c), which permits declining novel or complex state issues, substantially predominant state claims, cases in which all original-jurisdiction claims are dismissed, and exceptional circumstances giving other compelling reasons. The refiling here satisfies the federal period; substantive state tort law remains operative.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Raygor’s immune state-law claims outside §1367(a) remain outside the linked tolling rule. Covered county claims do not acquire the same exclusion by labeling limitations an immunity.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse the limitations judgment and remand for application of the actual filing and dismissal record and remaining preserved issues affecting the $80,000 verdict. The federal civil-rights summary judgment remains intact. The statutory rule applies to still-open cases within its scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** McCulloch supplies adapted means, without absolute necessity. New York distinguishes legislative commands from state-court application of valid federal law. Raygor retains its excluded-State-claim predicate. Syngenta’s demand for an actual jurisdictional source is satisfied. Monell supplies the municipality–State distinction; Alden and Florida Prepaid retain their actual expressly authorized federal-enforcement holdings.

## Current-term public authority: united_states_v_holston_merits_2003-10-30.md

Effective: 2003-10-30. Date gate: All five matters.

## Event

United States v. Holston; Second Circuit No. 02-1292; judgment below reported at 343 F.3d 83. Merits decision, October 30, 2003, October Term 2003.

On merits submission for review of the Second Circuit's judgment affirming Holston's conviction following a conditional guilty plea. The plea preserved whether prior interstate movement of recording materials alone constitutionally supports this local production prosecution under 18 U.S.C. §2251(a), and whether including that production is otherwise necessary to the valid interstate image-market prohibition. Holston seeks invalidation of the application and relief from his conviction; the United States seeks affirmance. The record concerns recordings sexually exploiting actual minors, produced locally with equipment or media that had crossed state lines.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at merits submission and decision.

## Public Action

The Court affirms the Second Circuit's judgment against the preserved Commerce Clause challenge.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Disposition:** Affirmed, 9–0, against the preserved Commerce Clause challenge. Holston's requested dismissal of §2251(a) as applied and relief from his conviction are denied on the supported necessary-inclusion ground.

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The conditional plea and conviction remain effective. The case returns for ordinary implementation of the affirmed judgment, leaving any independently live sentencing proceedings to their existing course.

## Opinion Topology

O'CONNOR, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which STONE-ZSELA, C. J., and STEVENS, SCALIA, KENNEDY, SOUTER, THOMAS, GINSBURG, and BREYER, JJ., joined.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Affirms the judgment | Both controlling holdings, their explanations and application, and the entire judgment and remedy |

## Holdings

#### I. The statutory materials condition and the constitutional connection perform different work

**Controlling proposition:** The prior interstate movement of ordinary recording equipment or media does not, standing alone, supply constitutional authority for prohibiting the later wholly intrastate production of child pornography. That movement can satisfy the materials-in-commerce element of 18 U.S.C. §2251(a), which remains independently required in this prosecution; constitutional authority must rest on a sufficient relationship between the regulated production class and interstate commerce.

**Authority:** O'Connor's unanimous opinion of the Court. The common coalition identified in Opinion Topology directly joins both holdings and their explanations at the stated level of generality.

**Controlling explanation:** United States v. Lopez requires a constitutionally identifiable connection before aggregate magnitude can support federal authority. United States v. Griffin and United States v. Langley distinguish an enacted historical-movement condition from the constitutional basis for regulating the ensuing local class. The fact that a recording tool once crossed a state line proves its provenance. It does not itself explain how the later local production operates within interstate commerce or why its regulation is necessary to an interstate restriction. Treating that fact as sufficient would connect ordinary local conduct to federal power through the history of commonplace tools.

The express statutory connection therefore answers one inquiry but cannot complete the other. Holston's established materials movement satisfies the statutory condition used in his prosecution. The independently sufficient constitutional ground is the supported relationship between production and the prohibited image market explained below. That ground preserves the enacted element rather than deleting it or adding a defendant-specific sale, transmission or substantial-interstate-effect element.

#### II. Local production of actual-child-abuse images may be included in the supported interstate prohibition

**Controlling proposition:** The Commerce Clause together with the Necessary and Proper Clause permits Congress to prohibit local production of images exploiting actual children when excluding that production would permit evasion or material impairment of a valid prohibition of the interstate market in those images; including that production is then a reasonably adapted and integral means of executing the prohibition. The Government must identify the valid prohibition, the covered production class and their genuine relationship from the statute's operation and any supporting legislative or adjudicative basis; the court independently determines those constitutional boundaries and the class's reasonable fit, while Congress receives substantial latitude on reasonable empirical predictions and practical regulatory design.

**Authority:** The same unanimous opinion and common coalition. The rule and its application are directly majority-supported, without a fractured-decision inference.

**Controlling explanation:** United States v. Hale permits local conduct to be included when its exclusion would undermine an identified interstate restriction. United States v. Kirk applies that rule to local creation and retention of the very stock the regime prohibits, without requiring an individual sale. National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt permits inclusion of a local class that is a reasonably adapted and integral means of executing a valid interstate regulation, and requires identification of the regime, the covered class and a genuine functional relationship between them.

The required relationship exists here. Local production creates the actual-abuse images whose interstate circulation the federal regime prohibits. Those images can be reproduced, concealed and substituted for other images serving the same demand. Excluding their production would leave the source of replacement and additional supply outside the restriction and provide a material avenue around the interstate prohibition. The actual recordings, actual children and identity between the produced material and the prohibited supply support that conclusion. It is an inference from the product and the regime's operation, rather than a finding that Holston distributed his recordings.

Holston's objection that his production was local and noneconomic does not defeat this necessary-inclusion ground. The class's demonstrated source role, rather than a particular producer's completed sale, explains the connection. Nor does the Court rest on marketability alone or the statute's comprehensiveness: under Home Builders a declared national objective or the assembly of provisions into one statute does not establish the relationship. Here the characteristics of the produced material supply that relationship directly. Its identification requires neither universal formal legislative findings nor a fixed numerical benchmark or clear-and-convincing proof. The obligation remains the Government's; legislative latitude operates after the eligible mechanism is identified.

**Application and remedy:** The production of Holston's actual-child-abuse recordings falls within that supported class. The constitutional challenge to §2251(a) as applied fails, and the judgment sustaining his conviction is affirmed.

**Scope and questions outside the grant:** The holding addresses production of the actual-child-abuse material covered by the identified interstate prohibition. Distinct possession offenses and virtual imagery are outside the question presented; their treatment is not decided. Application of the necessary-inclusion rule to new production records is ordinary application of settled law, not a reservation of the rule.

## Precedent Treatment

- **United States v. Lopez, April 26, 1995:** Applied and reaffirmed. An eligible interstate connection must precede aggregation; equipment provenance cannot replace the required connection. Its constitutional boundary remains effective when an offense contains jurisdictional language.
- **United States v. Hale, February 12, 1996:** Applied. Its reasonably necessary inclusion rule reaches a local class only through a supported relationship to a valid interstate regime; the actual-abuse-image source relationship supplies that relationship here.
- **United States v. Kirk, February 14, 1998:** Applied for the absence of a universal individual-sale prerequisite when local creation and retention concern the prohibited stock. Its requirement of a fitted regime relationship retains full force.
- **National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt, June 8, 1998:** Applied for its necessary-inclusion rule, the Government's obligation to identify the regime, the covered class and a genuine functional relationship, independent judicial determination of those boundaries and respect for reasonable congressional judgments. Its wildlife application rests on the Act's integrated scheme; the relationship here rests on the supported product-and-source relationship in this record.
- **Hiley v. Barrett, October 9, 1998:** Applied for the method of identifying the practical relationship between the regulated class and a valid supply restriction. Its recipient-possession application remains distinct from the production class decided here.
- **United States v. Franklyn and United States v. Gonzalez, October 22, 1998:** Applied for the distinction between an enacted nexus and a supported supply-regime justification. Their supply-and-recipient mechanism retains its own statutory scope.
- **United States v. Griffin and United States v. Langley, October 29, 1998:** Applied to preserve the separate work of the enacted historical-movement element and the constitutional mechanism. The existence or satisfaction of one does not supply or eliminate the other.

## Law After Decision

Effective October 30, 2003, the supported necessary-inclusion doctrine sustains the defined local production class when actual-child-abuse images constitute the reproducible, concealable and substitutable supply of the identified interstate prohibition. Lower courts must identify the regime, the covered production class and its anti-evasion or material-impairment relationship to that regime, independently examine constitutional eligibility and fit, and give Congress latitude on reasonable empirical judgments. Proof of an individual interstate sale is unnecessary to that established class-and-regime ground. The statutory materials-movement element continues to govern the prosecution independently.

This decision adds a controlling application to the existing rule. Lopez's connection requirement, Home Builders's identification rule and Griffin/Langley's separation of statutory nexus from constitutional authority retain their force. The equipment-only theory is insufficient; the supported production mechanism sustains the challenged application.

## Separate Writings

## Procedure After Action

The mandate issues in the ordinary course. The lower court implements the affirmed judgment; the conditional plea and conviction remain effective, and any independently live sentencing proceedings retain their existing scope. The Supreme Court's merits review of the reserved constitutional challenge is concluded.

## Source Notes

United States v. Holston, 343 F.3d 83, Second Circuit No. 02-1292; U.S. Const., Art. I, §8, cls. 3 and 18; 18 U.S.C. §2251(a).


## Current-term public authority: united_states_v_ho_merits_2003-11-20.md

Effective: 2003-11-20. Date gate: All five matters.

## Event

United States v. Ho; judgment below, 311 F.3d 589. Merits decision, November 20, 2003, on merits submission. The Court reviews the Commerce Clause validity of applying the Clean Air Act's asbestos-removal work-practice and advance-notification requirements to Ho's intrastate commercial renovation. Ho bought a former hospital after asbestos disclosure, rejected licensed abatement bids and procured substitute paid removal work. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the two convictions, separately vacated the sentence and remanded. For the constitutional question it assumed that asbestos had not escaped; the sentence involved a distinct release inquiry.

## Participation

Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at submission and decision.

## Public Action

The conviction component is affirmed against the Commerce Clause challenge. The separately ordered sentencing proceedings remain in effect.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Convictions affirmed against the preserved constitutional challenge, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The work-practice and notification convictions remain effective. The Fifth Circuit's distinct sentence vacatur and remand retain their existing grounds and scope; the original sentence is not reinstated. Acquittals and dismissed counts remain undisturbed.

## Opinion Topology

STONE-ZSELA, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which STEVENS, O'CONNOR, SCALIA, KENNEDY, SOUTER, THOMAS, GINSBURG, and BREYER, JJ., joined.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Complete direct-market, preventive-regulation and ancillary-notice grounds; both conviction components and sentence-remand limit |

## Holdings

### I. The regulated removal work directly participates in an interstate service market

**Controlling proposition:** Congress may regulate the asbestos-removal work practices in this commercial renovation because the regulated operation itself is produced and procured in an established interstate abatement-service market. Once that direct economic relationship and the enacted class's fit are supported, Congress may assess the class's aggregate market effects without requiring the individual project to produce an independently substantial interstate effect.

**Authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion, joined by all eight Associate Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Lopez requires a connection before magnitude; Wickard and Perez permit aggregate assessment of an actual economic class, and Hodel permits regulation of economic operations for environmental ends. Ho's licensed bids, cost-based rejection and paid substitute workers identify the very service whose production and cost the work standards regulate. Repeated avoidance of required precautions changes competitive abatement costs. Direct performance substituted for purchased abatement remains part of that service-market activity.

The enacted provisions regulate asbestos-removal work during covered facility renovation and the notice supporting it. Facility coverage reaches institutional, commercial, public and industrial structures, specified residential structures including condominiums and cooperatives, ships and active or inactive waste sites. It excludes apartment buildings of four or fewer units, does not classify a structure with a loft dwelling as residential on that account, and retains coverage of previously covered structures despite later use changes. Ho's hospital coverage is uncontested. This breadth is not rewritten as a commercial-building element.

Ho's strongest objection is that Home Builders forbids selecting a commercial project to disguise a differently defined noneconomic class. That rule remains controlling. Here removal itself is the procured and performed service, rather than unrelated conduct occurring within an owner's commercial surroundings. Property value and ownership do not supply the bridge. The demonstrated operation-level connection supports this application without adding a commerce element to the offense. Generalized national health costs do no work in that conclusion.

### II. Preventive work standards and their notice duty may precede release

**Controlling proposition:** Valid regulation of the identified economic removal operation may prescribe preventive practices and advance notice without proof that the particular project released asbestos into ambient air or across a state boundary. The notice duty is sustained as directly ancillary to enforcement of those work standards; the Government must still establish the enacted offense elements beyond a reasonable doubt.

**Authority:** The same unanimous opinion.

**Controlling explanation:** Preventive standards regulate how the economic service is performed before the feared release occurs. Advance notice allows administration and enforcement at that stage. Requiring a proved cross-border injury would treat prevention as constitutionally unavailable even though the regulated activity already has the necessary market relationship. The absence of an actual release, assumed for this question, therefore does not defeat the power to regulate these practices and notice obligations.

The notice holding concerns its fitted relationship to the regulated operation, rather than aggregation of failures to report in general. An actual-release condition in a different offense retains its own role, and the separate sentencing finding under a different evidentiary standard supplies no element here. Holston's supported inclusion of local image production in a national prohibition remains a distinct mechanism: this direct service-market ground does not depend on importing its concealment, reproducibility or supply predicates. The constitutional validity of the separate sentence enhancements is outside the granted question.

## Precedent Treatment

- United States v. Lopez: applied to connection before aggregation, the actual regulated class and the prohibition on adding an unexpressed commerce element.
- National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt: applied and distinguished because this regulation addresses the actual abatement operation, rather than relying on commercial surroundings to characterize unrelated conduct; its identification-and-fit rule remains effective.
- Wickard v. Filburn: applied to class-wide effects of supported economic activity without an independently substantial effect from each instance.
- Perez v. United States: applied to class-wide effects of supported economic activity without an independently substantial effect from each instance.
- Hodel v. Virginia Surface Mining & Reclamation Association: applied to environmental regulation of an actual economic operation.
- United States v. Holston: preserved at its supported production-and-regime scope; the present direct-market holding uses a different established mechanism.

## Law After Decision

The Commerce Clause permits preventive asbestos-removal and fitted advance-notice duties for the commercial removal operation supported here, without an individual release or cross-border-injury requirement. Courts must identify the regulated conduct and its supported direct market relationship before aggregation. The decision adds this application to existing Commerce doctrine; the enacted-class limitation and the requirement of proof of the statutory offenses remain effective.

## Separate Writings



## Procedure After Action

The lower court implements the affirmed convictions and conducts the separately ordered sentencing proceedings within their preserved scope under existing jury-finding, acquittal and procedural rules.

## Source Notes

United States v. Ho, 311 F.3d 589; 42 U.S.C. §§7412(h), 7414(a), 7413(c)(1) and 7413(c)(2)(B); 40 C.F.R. §§61.141 and 61.145. The constitutional question proceeds on the assumed absence of actual asbestos escape; the separate sentencing discharge finding has a different procedural and evidentiary basis.


## Current-term public authority: united_states_v_deaton_merits_2003-12-11.md

Effective: 2003-12-11. Date gate: All five matters.

## Event

United States v. Deaton; judgment below, 332 F.3d 698. Merits decision, December 11, 2003, on merits submission. The Court reviews the Fourth Circuit’s affirmance of Clean Water Act jurisdiction, the wetland determination and an order to refill the excavated ditch and restore previolation elevation. The questions concern statutory coverage of wetlands adjoining the demonstrated tributary system, Congress’s channel-protection power, the Corps’ hydrology method and the restoration alternative. The earlier sidecasting-discharge ruling is settled. The wetlands adjoin a roadside ditch draining through a culvert, the John Adkins Prong of Perdue Creek and Beaverdam Creek to the navigable Wicomico River and Chesapeake Bay. The route is agreed; the amount and consistency of flow are disputed.

## Participation

Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at merits submission and decision.

## Public Action

The judgment is affirmed on all four reviewed components.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Affirmed, 9–0, on statutory coverage, constitutional authority, delineation and restoration.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The district court’s order requiring refilling of the ditch and restoration of previolation elevation remains effective under its existing terms, schedule and oversight.

## Opinion Topology

KENNEDY, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which STEVENS, O'CONNOR, SCALIA, SOUTER, THOMAS, GINSBURG, and BREYER, JJ., joined. STONE-ZSELA, C. J., joined the statutory coverage conclusion in Part I, all of Part II and the operative restoration mandate in Part IV, and concurred in the judgment on Part III without adding a ground.

| Lead-opinion component | Justices joining the stated rationale | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| I, conclusion that the demonstrated tributary-connected wetlands are covered | All nine | Common statutory coverage proposition |
| I, delegated statutory choice and own-regulation interpretation | Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Eight complete rationale joins |
| II, channel protection | All nine | Complete controlling rationale |
| III, wetland delineation | Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Eight rationale joins; Stone-Zsela concurs in this component’s judgment without adding a ground |
| IV, restoration | Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Eight complete rationale joins; Stone-Zsela joins the operative restoration mandate |

## Holdings

### I. The Act and valid regulations reach this connected system

**Controlling proposition:** The Clean Water Act and the Corps’ tributary and adjacent-wetland regulations cover these wetlands adjoining the demonstrated feeder system into navigable waters. The statutory program delegates authority exercised through binding regulations; the permissible inclusion of this connected system and the responsible Corps construction of tributaries as its feeder branches receive their respective controlling weight within statutory and regulatory limits.

**Authority:** Part I’s coverage conclusion has nine joins. Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer supply eight direct joins to the complete delegated-choice and regulatory-interpretation rationale; Stone-Zsela’s join is confined to the coverage conclusion.

**Controlling explanation:** Sections 1311, 1344 and 1362 establish the discharge prohibition, dredged-or-fill permit program and definition extending beyond navigability in fact. Section 1344 assigns the program to the Secretary of the Army acting through the Chief of Engineers, with structured permit, guideline, general-permit and state-administration provisions. Haggar and Mead require that actual assignment and its exercise before deference; Barnhart applies the same sequence in a different statutory program. Ambiguity or expertise alone does not confer authority.

The Corps reasonably includes this connected tributary system and its conceded adjacent wetlands under section 328.3(a)(1), (5) and (7). The latter provision covers wetlands adjacent to the identified waters other than waters themselves wetlands. Riverside Bayview preserves adjacent-wetland coverage. SWANCC’s bird-use-only isolated-pond limit does not impose the owners’ proposed direct-feeder boundary on this supported connection.

The distinct question about the regulation’s meaning receives Auer’s fair-and-considered-interpretation rule. Tributaries reasonably includes feeder branches reaching navigable water through intermediate streams; the responsible Corps construction is consistent with that text. Earlier primary, secondary and tertiary usage confirms the meaning. A former headwaters coverage cutoff did not establish that more remote branches were linguistically never tributaries. The direct-feeder alternative is plausible but not compelled. Neither form of deference proves hydrological facts, permits interpretive amendment or displaces the Government’s ordinary civil burdens. The actual route and conceded adjacency supply the application here, rather than environmental importance alone.

### II. Protection of the receiving navigable channel supports this application

**Controlling proposition:** Congress may prevent pollutant effects in an identified navigable waterway by regulating the established discharge class in its demonstrated tributary system and adjacent wetlands. The Government must support that connection and mechanism; once established, the channel ground requires neither an independently substantial effect from this individual fill nor tracing a particular particle into the receiving river.

**Authority:** Part II, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Lopez preserves direct protection of interstate channels and requires a real connection before aggregate magnitude can do work. Rio Grande Dam, Appalachian Electric Power, Oklahoma ex rel. Phillips and Grand River Dam support protection of navigable waters through relevant nonnavigable reaches; Caminetti recognizes protection against harmful channel uses. The power is not confined to clearing obstructions from boat passage.

The agreed drainage route connects the roadside ditch and adjacent wetlands to the Wicomico. The Corps supplied evidence that discharges into the connected tributaries and adjacent wetlands substantially affect receiving-water quality; the owners did not contend that the reported class effect was overstated. The approximately eight-mile route to the navigable river, intermediate ponds and dams, and disputed flow consistency therefore require attention but do not erase this supported connection. A particular parcel’s small contribution does not defeat prevention directed to that connected class.

The owners’ strongest objection is that remote drainage can turn channel protection into general land-use power. The answer is the established receiving channel, actual route and supported discharge mechanism, rather than a presumption that every ditch connects or national environmental concern. Home Builders retains a separate externality route. The externality route requires identification of the regulated class; a concrete cross-border ecological, commercial or comparable interstate effect; why that effect is substantial rather than speculative or merely nationally interesting; why the affected States cannot reasonably internalize or control it through ordinary territorial authority; and the reasonable fit of the federal prohibition to that effect. Drainage alone does not establish those conditions. The supported channel ground fully sustains this application.

### III. The root-zone indicator answers the preserved Manual objection

**Controlling proposition:** Section 328.3(b) requires inundation or saturation by surface or groundwater at a frequency and duration sufficient to support, and under normal circumstances actually supporting, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted to saturated soils. Within that complete definition, the Manual’s express visual indicator of saturation in a major part of the root zone, usually within twelve inches, defeats the asserted requirement of saturation to the surface; the Corps’ determination is sustained on this preserved interpretation issue.

**Authority:** Part III, joined by all eight Associate Justices. Stone-Zsela concurs in affirmance of this component without adding a ground.

**Controlling explanation:** The 1987 Manual applies vegetation, hydric-soil and hydrology criteria, with recorded water data ranked above field indicators. Its specific root-zone indicator explains how saturation can have the overriding effect on vegetation relevant to wetland hydrology. The owners’ twenty-two-well monitoring argument relied on inadequate saturation to the surface. Reading the general surface description with the express indicator answers their contention that the Corps contradicted the Manual. Vegetation and hydric soil are undisputed, and the described challenge establishes no contrary root-zone measurement requiring this Court to resolve a factual conflict.

Auer permits the responsible, text-consistent regulatory explanation; it does not allow a scientific manual to amend the regulation or make one observation conclusive. Frequency, duration, normal circumstances and the actual vegetation criterion remain essential. Genuinely contrary higher-ranked data must retain their proper weight. The claim that the Manual itself is inconsistent with the regulation was not presented. Affirmance thus resolves the asserted misuse of its language while preserving the complete regulatory conditions.

### IV. Refilling reasonably restores the established violation’s effects

**Controlling proposition:** A restoration order must bear an equitable relationship to the actual violation, be practically achievable and serve restoration of the affected environment. The district court did not abuse its discretion by requiring refilling and previolation elevation rather than removal of the sidecast soil elsewhere, because the proposed removal would preserve the unlawful project’s drainage benefit and risk further ecological harm.

**Authority:** Part IV’s complete rationale has the eight Associate joins. All nine support the operative restoration mandate; Stone-Zsela’s agreement is confined to that operative remedial scope.

**Controlling explanation:** The owners emphasize that digging alone was not the established discharge and that hauling the soil to nonwetland land could have avoided a violation initially. But an option that would have avoided a violation before the work does not necessarily restore the affected wetlands afterward. The actual findings explain both the retained drainage benefit and the risk of further harm from the proposed removal. Those concrete reasons connect the ordered refilling to the previolation condition.

Cumberland Farms supplies persuasive considerations of environmental benefit, feasibility and equitable relation rather than a compulsory checklist. The Act’s restoration objective supports the properly bounded choice; it does not establish a separate prohibition on excavation or authority over unrelated land use. The existing order remains tied to this discharge and its effects, and ordinary enforcement must address any supported feasibility or compliance issue on its evidence.

## Precedent Treatment

- United States v. Riverside Bayview Homes: applied to adjacent-wetland coverage within the enacted water program.
- Solid Waste Agency of Northern Cook County v. United States Army Corps of Engineers: distinguished because this application rests on a demonstrated tributary connection, preserving its bird-use-only isolated-pond limit.
- United States v. Haggar Apparel Co.: applied to actual delegated authority and independent enforcement of statutory limits before controlling deference.
- United States v. Mead Corp.: applied to actual delegation and its exercise through a mechanism carrying the force of law before controlling deference.
- Barnhart v. Thomas: applied to that delegation-first sequence without transferring its Social Security statutory assignment to the Corps.
- Auer v. Robbins: applied separately to the responsible, fair and text-consistent regulatory construction, preserving the distinction between interpretation and factual proof.
- United States v. Lopez: applied to the direct channel-protection ground and the need for a supported connection before aggregation.
- United States v. Rio Grande Dam & Irrigation Co.: applied to protection of navigable water against upstream interference.
- United States v. Appalachian Electric Power Co.: applied to protection of navigable waters through relevant nonnavigable reaches.
- Oklahoma ex rel. Phillips v. Guy F. Atkinson Co.: applied to protection of navigable waters through relevant nonnavigable reaches.
- United States v. Grand River Dam Authority: applied to protection of navigable waters through relevant nonnavigable reaches.
- Caminetti v. United States: applied to protection of navigable channels against harmful uses.
- National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt: its separate interstate-externality requirements remain effective; the channel ground independently resolves this application.

## Law After Decision

The demonstrated tributary system and its adjacent wetlands fall within the valid water program, and supported protection of the navigable receiving channel sustains this discharge application. Statutory delegation, regulatory interpretation, factual hydrology and constitutional authority remain distinct inquiries. The complete wetland definition continues to govern use of the root-zone indicator. Restoration requires its own equitable and practical justification, supplied here by the actual findings supporting refilling.

## Separate Writings



## Procedure After Action

The affirmed restoration order remains enforceable under the district court’s actual terms, schedule and oversight. The owners must refill the ditch and restore previolation elevation as ordered. Supported questions about feasibility or compliance must be resolved from the order and the evidence in ordinary enforcement.

## Source Notes

United States v. Deaton, 332 F.3d 698; 33 U.S.C. §§1251(a), 1311, 1344 and 1362; 33 C.F.R. §328.3(a)(1), (5), (7), (b) and (c); United States v. Cumberland Farms of Connecticut, Inc., 826 F.2d 1151, 1164. The existence of the drainage route is agreed while flow amount and consistency are disputed. The preserved Manual challenge concerns its application, with vegetation and hydric soil uncontested.


## Current-term public authority: rancho_viejo_llc_v_norton_merits_2004-02-05.md

Effective: 2004-02-05. Date gate: Carnes only; excluded from the four January events.

## Event

Rancho Viejo, LLC v. Norton; D.C. Circuit No. 01-5373; judgment below reported at 323 F.3d 1062. Merits decision, February 5, 2004, October Term 2003.

On merits submission for review of the D.C. Circuit's April 1, 2003 judgment, rehearing denied July 22, 2003. The question is whether the Commerce Clause authorizes application of the Endangered Species Act's wildlife-taking prohibition to a commercial housing development threatening a species found entirely within one State. The proposed 202-acre San Diego County development threatens the arroyo toad. The circuit sustained the application by treating the commercial development as the regulated activity. Rancho Viejo seeks reversal and relief against the application; the federal officials seek affirmance.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at submission and decision.

## Public Action

The Court affirms the D.C. Circuit's judgment sustaining the challenged application against the Commerce Clause objection, on the necessary-inclusion ground of National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Disposition:** Affirmed, 9–0, against the Commerce Clause challenge. The D.C. Circuit's judgment sustaining the challenged application of the taking prohibition stands on the necessary-inclusion ground, not on the circuit's commercial-project ground.

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The judgment sustaining the application against Rancho Viejo's Commerce Clause objection remains in effect, and Rancho Viejo's requested relief against the application is denied. The Government may enforce the taking prohibition in this application subject to its actual elements and exceptions. Whether the proposed development will cause a prohibited taking remains governed by the statute's injury and causation requirements, and any section 10 permission or other independently pending statutory issue retains its ordinary procedural posture.

## Opinion Topology

KENNEDY, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which STONE-ZSELA, C. J., and O'CONNOR, SCALIA, THOMAS, GINSBURG, and BREYER, JJ., joined, and in which STEVENS and SOUTER, JJ., joined as to Parts II and III. STEVENS, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment, in which SOUTER, J., joined.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer; Stevens and Souter as to Parts II and III | Affirms | Part I: enacted taking class and rejection of the commercial-project ground (seven Justices); Part II: necessary inclusion under Home Builders sustains the taking prohibition as applied to the arroyo toad (nine); Part III: affirmance, with the statutory questions left to their own rules (nine) |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stevens | Souter | Joins Parts II and III and the judgment | Additional economic-application ground for affirmance and proposed reconsideration of Home Builders's contrary class ruling at that scope; does not join Part I |

## Holdings

### I. A commercial project does not replace the statutory taking class

**Controlling proposition:** The commercial character of a housing project does not by itself establish Congress's authority to apply the Endangered Species Act's wildlife-taking prohibition. The Government must identify an eligible interstate mechanism fitted to the taking class Congress enacted, including the habitat-caused injury that class reaches.

**Authority:** Part I of Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Those seven Justices directly join this holding and its explanation; Stevens and Souter join Parts II and III and the judgment but not this part.

**Controlling explanation:** National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt governs this question. Section 9 prohibits taking protected wildlife without making a project's commercial character the defining condition of the prohibition. United States v. Lopez requires a constitutionally sufficient connection for that enacted class before aggregation can measure its effects.

The D.C. Circuit relied on Rancho Viejo's commercial housing development as the regulated activity. The development is commercial, and the contrary view correctly identifies habitat conversion itself, rather than an incidental purchase, as the injury-producing conduct. But Home Builders already considered and rejected that feature as an independently sufficient connection for the enacted taking class. Describing the challenge as applied to this project does not remove the need to identify the mechanism that connects the prohibition to interstate commerce. The Court applies that existing rule.

Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon supplies the statutory treatment of habitat-caused injury. It does not supply the separate constitutional connection. Wickard v. Filburn and Perez v. United States permit class-wide assessment within properly connected economic classes; under Home Builders they do not make this project's commercial character a substitute for the required connection.

### II. The taking prohibition, as applied to the arroyo toad, is an integral part of the Act's valid interstate scheme

**Controlling proposition:** Under National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt, Congress may regulate intrastate conduct that is neither itself interstate commerce nor independently shown to have substantial interstate effects when inclusion of the regulated class is a reasonably adapted and integral means of executing an otherwise valid federal regulation of interstate commerce. The Endangered Species Act's integrated system regulating interstate exploitation, movement and commercial disposition of listed wildlife may include the unauthorized taking of listed wildlife as a means of preserving the populations and enforceability of that system, without separate proof that each species crosses state boundaries, participates in interstate commerce or would independently produce a substantial interstate commercial effect. The section 9(a)(1)(B) taking prohibition, as applied to the listed arroyo toad within that system, falls within Congress's Commerce and Necessary and Proper powers; Rancho Viejo has not shown that the application is outside the statutory class, that the Act's interstate regulation is not independently valid, or that the relationship is nominal or pretextual.

**Authority:** Parts II and III of Kennedy's opinion of the Court are joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine Justices directly join this holding, its explanation and the affirmance.

**Controlling explanation:** Home Builders supplies the rule and its unit of analysis. The Commerce Clause, with the Necessary and Proper Clause, lets Congress select means reasonably adapted to the effective execution of a valid regulation of commerce among the States; it does not require every included intrastate act to be independently regulable. The unit is the taking prohibition within the federal scheme, not each species or local controversy.

The Act regulates the importation, exportation, interstate transport, sale and commercial handling of listed wildlife, the possession and shipment of unlawfully taken wildlife, the taking of listed wildlife and permissible incidental taking. The taking prohibition protects the populations whose exploitation and interstate movement those provisions govern and keeps the provisions enforceable. Home Builders sustained it as applied to the Delhi Sands flower-loving fly, a species found in one State and absent from trade.

That holding governs this application. The challenged application concerns habitat modification that section 9(a)(1)(B) reaches, as Sweet Home construes it, when the modification actually kills or injures listed wildlife. The Act's valid interstate regulation, the covered class and the protective function connecting them appear from the statute's operation, so the toad's intrastate range and the absence of an established market in it do not defeat the application. Rancho Viejo identifies no feature placing this application outside the class, no defect in the Act's interstate regulation and nothing nominal or pretextual in the relationship. United States v. Holston applied necessary inclusion to the reproducible supply of a prohibited interstate image market; this application rests on the Act's own wildlife scheme, not on a transferred market analogy.

The rule keeps an enforceable distinction between the commerce power and a general police power. Congress cannot establish the relationship by declaring a national objective or assembling unrelated provisions into one statute, and biodiversity's general importance, speculative scientific or future economic value, tourism and development pressure do not supply it. Aggregation measures magnitude only after a constitutionally eligible connection exists. Because necessary inclusion establishes congressional power here, Home Builders's independent externality route need not be satisfied.

### III. The judgment sustaining the challenged application is affirmed

**Controlling proposition:** When a judgment sustaining an application of the taking prohibition rests on the insufficient commercial-project ground but Home Builders's necessary-inclusion rule sustains the same application on the statute's text and structure, the judgment is affirmed on that ground, and no Commerce Clause evidentiary remand is required. The D.C. Circuit's judgment sustaining application of section 9 to the arroyo toad against Rancho Viejo's Commerce Clause objection is affirmed.

**Authority:** The same nine-Justice Parts II and III control the disposition.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court reviews the judgment, not only its reasoning. The commercial ground below cannot sustain the application, but the necessary-inclusion ground does, and it rests on the Act's text and structure and the record already before the Court. A further hearing on the local toad would leave the constitutional question unsettled without bearing on the relationship that sustains the application. Rancho Viejo's requested relief against the application is therefore denied.

Whether the proposed development will cause a prohibited taking remains governed by Sweet Home's statutory injury, proximate-cause and foreseeability requirements. Any section 10 permission and any independently pending statutory or permitting issue retain their own statutory conditions and ordinary procedural posture.

**Application and remedy:** The D.C. Circuit's judgment sustaining the challenged application is affirmed. The Government may enforce the taking prohibition in this application subject to its actual elements and exceptions.

## Precedent Treatment

- **National Association of Home Builders v. Babbitt, June 8, 1998:** Reaffirmed and applied. Its enacted taking class and rejection of project commerce as independently sufficient govern Part I. Its necessary-inclusion rule sustains the taking prohibition as applied to the listed toad within the Act's integrated system, without species-by-species, border-crossing or independent-effects proof, subject to its outside-class, invalid-regime and pretext showings, its identification rule, independent judicial determination of the legal boundaries and respect for reasonable congressional judgments. Its independent externality route remains available but need not be satisfied.
- **United States v. Lopez, April 26, 1995:** Applied. The constitutional connection precedes magnitude, must fit the enacted class and must leave an enforceable boundary; neither project commerce nor insertion of an unexpressed commerce element supplies the required inquiry.
- **United States v. Holston, October 30, 2003:** Applied for the necessary-inclusion method and distinguished on its actual image-supply relationship. Its demonstrated mechanism supplies no presumed wildlife market or ecological spillover; this application rests on the Act's integrated wildlife scheme.
- **United States v. Hale, February 12, 1996:** Preserved. Its machinegun holding supplies a different example of necessary inclusion within an identified valid interstate regime; no machinegun-specific premise is imported into conservation law.
- **United States v. Kirk, February 14, 1998:** Preserved for a fitted prohibited-stock relationship without a universal individual-sale requirement. Its specific stock relationship is not imported into conservation law; the relationship here lies in the Act's own scheme.
- **Wickard v. Filburn, 317 U.S. 111:** Preserved for aggregation within a properly connected economic class; it does not displace Home Builders's enacted-class rule.
- **Perez v. United States, 402 U.S. 146:** Preserved for class-wide assessment of connected economic conduct without a separately substantial effect from each act; it does not create a missing connection through this project's commerce.
- **Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, June 29, 1995:** Preserved as the separate statutory rule. Significant habitat modification must actually kill or injure protected wildlife through significant impairment of essential behavior, including breeding, feeding or sheltering, with proximate causation and ordinary foreseeability. Speculative harm and bare but-for linkage are insufficient; an omission requires an independent legal duty, and otherwise lawful development alone is no exemption. Those statutory conditions remain distinct from constitutional authority and from any section 10 permission.

## Law After Decision

Effective February 5, 2004, Home Builders's necessary-inclusion rule sustains the Endangered Species Act's section 9(a)(1)(B) taking prohibition as applied to listed wildlife within the Act's integrated system, including an application to a commercial project threatening a species found only in one State, without separate proof that the species crosses state boundaries, participates in interstate commerce or independently produces a substantial interstate commercial effect. A challenger may show that an application is outside the statutory class, that the Act's interstate regulation is not independently valid, or that the relationship is nominal or pretextual. A project's commercial character does not itself supply the connection for the enacted taking class, and the independent externality route remains available on its own requirements.

The commercial-project rationale cannot alone sustain this application; the necessary-inclusion ground sustains it, and the judgment below stands. This decision applies the existing doctrine without creating a new Commerce category.

## Separate Writings

**Stevens, concurring in part and concurring in the judgment, joined by Souter.** They join Parts II and III and the judgment. The Court's necessary-inclusion ground sustains this application of the taking prohibition, as they agreed in Home Builders. They would also affirm on a further ground: the activity directly producing the alleged habitat injury is commercial housing construction and land conversion. Sweet Home identifies that physical habitat alteration as the conduct reached by the taking prohibition. Their additional ground therefore looks to the actual economic application, rather than to the developer's collateral equipment purchases or a generalized claim that species preservation benefits the national economy.

Wickard and Perez permit class-wide regulation of connected economic activity, and Hodel v. Virginia Surface Mining & Reclamation Association permits regulation of economic land use for environmental ends. On that reasoning, the actual construction supplies a sufficient economic connection without a market in the toad or a newly found ecological spillover. They accept the continuing statutory requirements of actual habitat-caused injury and ordinary causation; their additional ground concerns the Commerce Clause challenge.

Home Builders's contrary enacted-class holding directly obstructs this ground, and they do not join Part I. Stevens and Souter would reconsider that holding to the extent it excludes reliance on the actual injury-producing economic activity in this application. They regard treating the prohibition's broader coverage as a reason to disregard this commercial application as a mistaken class inquiry. They neither claim that their earlier dissent already controls nor distinguish Home Builders through a new factual premise. Their ground is an additional reason for the same judgment; it would not make every noneconomic taking an economic activity.

## Procedure After Action

The D.C. Circuit's judgment sustaining the challenged application is affirmed, and the taking prohibition remains enforceable in that application subject to its actual elements and exceptions. Any section 10 permission and any independently pending statutory or permitting issue retain their ordinary procedural posture. Supreme Court merits review of the Commerce Clause challenge is complete.

## Source Notes

Rancho Viejo, LLC v. Norton, 323 F.3d 1062, D.C. Circuit No. 01-5373; U.S. Const., Art. I, §8, cls. 3 and 18; Endangered Species Act §§9 and 10, 16 U.S.C. §§1538 and 1539. The threatened project's commercial character does not itself establish a cross-border ecological effect or a mechanism of market evasion.
